stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with sudden severe headache and drooping of her left eyelid. The left eye looks down and out, and the left pupil is dilated and unreactive. Aneurysm of which artery most likely explains this?
explanation: The oculomotor nerve passes forwards between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries and runs alongside the posterior communicating artery, so an aneurysm here compresses it. The superficial parasympathetic fibres are affected early, giving a dilated pupil along with ptosis and the 'down and out' eye. Anterior communicating aneurysms are the commonest overall but cause visual field or frontal signs rather than a third nerve palsy.

stem: A 60-year-old diabetic man complains of double vision when walking down stairs and reading. He tilts his head to the left to reduce the diplopia. On testing, the right eye cannot look down when it is turned inwards. Which cranial nerve is affected?
explanation: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique, which depresses the adducted eye and intorts it; weakness causes vertical diplopia on looking down and in, as on stairs, and patients tilt the head away from the affected side to compensate. A right fourth nerve palsy therefore produces a left head tilt. A third nerve palsy would also cause ptosis and a down-and-out eye.

stem: A 25-year-old woman with idiopathic intracranial hypertension develops horizontal double vision. Her left eye cannot move outwards beyond the midline. Which nerve is most likely affected as a false localising sign?
explanation: The abducens nerve has a long intracranial course and bends sharply over the petrous apex, so it is easily stretched by raised intracranial pressure, producing lateral rectus weakness without a local lesion. The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique and causes vertical, not horizontal, diplopia.

stem: In a patient with a skull base tumour, touching the right cornea produces no blinking in either eye. Touching the left cornea makes both eyes blink normally. Where is the lesion?
explanation: The corneal reflex has its afferent limb in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve and its efferent limb in both facial nerves (consensual blink). Loss of both blinks when only the right cornea is touched, with a normal response from the left, means the right afferent is damaged. A right facial lesion would abolish only the right blink, whichever side is touched.

stem: A 68-year-old man has a stroke with weakness of the lower part of the right side of his face. He can wrinkle his forehead and close his eyes normally on both sides. Why is the forehead spared?
options: The forehead muscles are supplied by the trigeminal nerve
The upper facial nucleus has input from both hemispheres
The forehead is supplied by the opposite facial nerve
The temporal branch leaves the facial nerve before the brainstem
explanation: The part of the facial motor nucleus supplying the upper face receives corticobulbar fibres from both hemispheres, whereas the part supplying the lower face receives mainly contralateral input. An upper motor neurone lesion therefore spares the forehead, whereas a lower motor neurone (Bell's) palsy weakens the whole half of the face.

stem: A 35-year-old man develops weakness of the whole left half of his face, with loss of taste over the front of the left side of his tongue and discomfort from ordinary sounds in the left ear. Lacrimation is normal. Where is the lesion of the facial nerve?
options: At the stylomastoid foramen as the nerve leaves the skull base
Within the parotid gland among its terminal branches
At the cerebellopontine angle with the eighth nerve
In the facial canal just distal to the geniculate ganglion
explanation: Hyperacusis (stapedius paralysis) and loss of taste (chorda tympani) place the lesion above both branches in the facial canal, while normal lacrimation shows that the greater petrosal nerve, arising at the geniculate ganglion, is spared. A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen or in the parotid would spare taste and hearing.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has gradually progressive hearing loss and tinnitus in her right ear. MRI shows a tumour at the right cerebellopontine angle. Apart from the eighth nerve, which cranial nerve is most often affected early, producing a reduced corneal reflex?
explanation: A vestibular schwannoma enlarges in the cerebellopontine angle and compresses the trigeminal nerve, and an early sign is a reduced corneal reflex from loss of the afferent limb. The facial nerve is closely related to the eighth nerve but is surprisingly resistant, so facial weakness appears late.

stem: Touching the back of the pharynx with a tongue depressor produces gagging. Which cranial nerve carries the sensory (afferent) limb of this reflex?
options: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve
explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies general sensation to the oropharynx and posterior third of the tongue and forms the afferent limb of the gag reflex; the vagus supplies the pharyngeal muscles and forms the efferent limb. The trigeminal nerve supplies the oral cavity in front of the palatoglossal arch.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a right-sided jugular foramen tumour is asked to say 'aah'. To which side does the uvula deviate?
explanation: The vagus supplies the levator veli palatini through the pharyngeal plexus. With a right vagal lesion, the intact left palatal muscles pull the uvula towards the left, the healthy side. Deviation towards the lesion is the rule for the tongue in hypoglossal palsy, not for the uvula.

stem: After a lymph node biopsy from the posterior triangle of the neck, a 30-year-old man has difficulty shrugging his left shoulder and raising his arm above his head, and the left shoulder droops. Which nerve was damaged?
explanation: The spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially, embedded in the roof of investing fascia, and is easily injured in node biopsies; it supplies trapezius, which elevates the shoulder and rotates the scapula for overhead abduction. The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior and causes winging rather than shoulder droop.

stem: A 40-year-old man had a neck operation. When he protrudes his tongue it deviates to the right, and the right side of the tongue is wasted. Which nerve is damaged?
explanation: Each genioglossus pushes the tongue forwards and towards the opposite side; if the right genioglossus is paralysed, the unopposed left muscle pushes the tongue to the right, the side of the lesion. Wasting indicates a lower motor neurone lesion of the right hypoglossal nerve. The lingual nerve is sensory to the tongue.

stem: A 27-year-old man hits his forehead in a motorbike accident. He later notices clear fluid dripping from his nose and has lost his sense of smell. Fracture of which bone is most likely?
options: Orbital plate of the frontal bone
explanation: Olfactory nerve filaments pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid to the olfactory bulb, and a fracture here tears the dura and the filaments, causing CSF rhinorrhoea and anosmia. A petrous temporal fracture causes CSF otorrhoea and may injure the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has headaches and has been bumping into door frames on both sides. Visual field testing shows loss of both temporal fields. Where is the lesion?
explanation: Fibres from the nasal halves of both retinas, which receive the temporal visual fields, cross in the optic chiasm; a pituitary tumour pressing on the chiasm from below produces bitemporal hemianopia. An optic tract lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia.

stem: A 52-year-old man has a tumour in the right temporal lobe. Visual field testing shows loss of the upper left quadrant in both eyes. Which fibres are damaged?
options: Fibres of Meyer's loop in the right optic radiation
Upper fibres of the right optic radiation in the parietal lobe
Crossing fibres in the optic chiasm
Fibres of the left optic tract
explanation: Fibres carrying the contralateral upper quadrant of vision loop forwards around the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle (Meyer's loop), so a right temporal lesion causes a left superior homonymous quadrantanopia. Parietal lobe lesions affect the upper radiation fibres and cause inferior quadrant loss.

stem: Shining a light into the left eye of a patient produces no constriction of either pupil, but shining it into the right eye makes both pupils constrict. Where is the lesion?
explanation: Both pupils constrict when the right eye is lit, so both efferent pathways (oculomotor nerves) work. Failure of both direct and consensual responses when the left eye is lit means the afferent signal from that eye is lost, indicating a left optic nerve lesion. A left oculomotor lesion would abolish constriction of the left pupil whichever eye is lit.

stem: After a total thyroidectomy, a 42-year-old woman has a hoarse, weak voice. Damage to which nerve, closely related to the inferior thyroid artery, is the most likely cause?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove and is closely related to the inferior thyroid artery near the lower pole of the gland; it supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, so injury causes vocal cord palsy and hoarseness. The external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery.

stem: A professional qawwali singer has a thyroid lobectomy. Afterwards her speaking voice is normal, but she cannot reach high notes and her voice tires easily. Which nerve was most likely injured during ligation of the superior thyroid vessels?
explanation: The external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery to the upper pole and supplies cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal cords for high-pitched sounds; injury causes loss of pitch range and voice fatigue. The internal laryngeal nerve is sensory to the larynx above the cords.

stem: A 9-year-old girl has a painless midline swelling just below the hyoid bone that moves upwards when she sticks out her tongue. From which embryological structure does it arise?
explanation: The thyroid descends from the foramen caecum of the tongue through the thyroglossal duct, closely related to the hyoid; a remnant forms a midline cyst that moves upwards with tongue protrusion. Branchial cleft cysts lie laterally along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid.

stem: A 22-year-old man has a smooth, fluctuant, non-tender swelling in the left side of the neck at the anterior border of the upper third of sternocleidomastoid. Aspiration yields turbid fluid with cholesterol crystals. What is its most likely embryological origin?
explanation: Branchial cysts are thought to arise from remnants of the second pharyngeal cleft and cervical sinus, and typically lie at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid at the junction of its upper and middle thirds; the fluid often contains cholesterol crystals. Thyroglossal cysts lie in the midline.

stem: During superficial parotidectomy for a pleomorphic adenoma, the surgeon identifies three main structures passing through the gland. Which is the most superficial and must be preserved?
explanation: Within the parotid gland, the facial nerve and its branches are the most superficial of the main structures, the retromandibular vein lies deeper, and the external carotid artery is deepest. The nerve's plane divides the superficial and deep lobes, so it is identified and preserved in parotid surgery.

stem: A 70-year-old man faints when his tight collar presses on the side of his neck at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. Stimulation of which structure is responsible?
explanation: The carotid sinus is a baroreceptor at the dilated origin of the internal carotid artery near the carotid bifurcation, at about the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage; pressure on it causes reflex bradycardia and hypotension through the glossopharyngeal nerve. The carotid body is a chemoreceptor responding to hypoxia.

stem: In an emergency airway, a doctor performs a needle cricothyroidotomy. Through which structure does the needle pass to enter the airway?
explanation: The cricothyroid membrane lies between the lower border of the thyroid cartilage and the arch of the cricoid, is superficial and relatively avascular, and lies below the vocal cords, so it is the access point in a 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' emergency. The thyrohyoid membrane is above the larynx.

stem: During an elective surgical tracheostomy in a ventilated adult, the surgeon encounters the isthmus of the thyroid gland. Over which tracheal rings does the isthmus usually lie?
explanation: The isthmus of the thyroid usually lies across the second to fourth tracheal rings and is retracted or divided to place the tracheostomy through the second to fourth rings. Placement through the first ring risks subglottic stenosis from damage to the cricoid.

stem: A newborn has recurrent infections, hypocalcaemic seizures and a conotruncal heart defect. Abnormal development of which embryological structures explains the immune and calcium problems?
options: First and second pharyngeal arch cartilages
explanation: In DiGeorge (22q11 deletion) syndrome the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches fail to develop properly; the third pouch forms the thymus and inferior parathyroids, and the fourth the superior parathyroids, so T-cell deficiency and hypocalcaemia result. The first pouch forms the middle ear cavity and auditory tube.

stem: A doctor inserts a central line into the right internal jugular vein using the central approach. Where is the needle inserted?
options: At the apex of the triangle between the two heads of sternocleidomastoid
Medial to the carotid pulse at the level of the cricoid
At the midpoint of the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid
Just above the middle of the clavicle in the posterior triangle of the neck
explanation: The internal jugular vein runs lateral to the common carotid artery and, low in the neck, lies beneath the triangle formed by the sternal and clavicular heads of sternocleidomastoid and the clavicle; the needle is inserted at the apex of this triangle, aimed towards the ipsilateral nipple. A needle medial to the carotid pulse would enter the artery or trachea.

stem: A 62-year-old right-handed man has a stroke. His speech is slow, effortful and halting with poor grammar, but he follows spoken instructions well and is aware of his errors. He also has weakness of the right side of the face and the right arm. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
explanation: Non-fluent (expressive) aphasia with preserved comprehension is Broca aphasia, from a lesion of Broca's area in the left inferior frontal gyrus, usually in the territory of the left middle cerebral artery; the adjacent motor cortex explains the right face and arm weakness. A lesion of the left superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's area) gives fluent speech with poor comprehension.

stem: A 30-year-old man has an infected scalp laceration. The surgeon warns that infection in one particular layer of the scalp can spread freely and reach the intracranial venous sinuses through emissary veins. Which layer is this?
explanation: The loose areolar tissue beneath the epicranial aponeurosis is the 'danger layer': it allows pus and blood to spread widely, and emissary veins crossing it connect the scalp veins with the dural venous sinuses. Infection in the dense connective tissue layer stays localised because the fibrous septa limit spread.

stem: A 24-year-old man squeezed a boil beside his nose. Five days later he has fever, proptosis and chemosis of the right eye, and he cannot move the right eye outwards. Which nerve is most likely the first to be affected in this condition, and why?
options: Oculomotor nerve, which lies in the lateral wall of the sinus
Abducens nerve, which lies free within the sinus beside the artery
Trochlear nerve, which is the thinnest of the cranial nerves
Ophthalmic nerve, which lies in the lateral wall of the sinus
explanation: Infection from the 'danger area' of the face reaches the cavernous sinus through the facial and ophthalmic veins, which lack effective valves. The abducens nerve runs through the body of the sinus beside the internal carotid artery, so it is usually affected first, whereas the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves lie in the lateral wall.

stem: A 76-year-old man who drinks heavily has had increasing confusion and headache over three weeks after a minor fall. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection over the left hemisphere. Which vessels are most likely the source of bleeding?
options: Bridging veins crossing the subdural space
Branches of the circle of Willis
explanation: Brain atrophy in older people and those with alcohol misuse stretches the bridging veins that cross from the cortex to the dural sinuses, so minor trauma tears them, producing a slowly enlarging crescent-shaped subdural haematoma. Middle meningeal artery injury causes an acute biconvex extradural haematoma.

stem: A 66-year-old right-handed woman with hypertension suddenly develops weakness of the right face and arm, with the right leg less affected, and she cannot find her words although she understands speech. Which artery is most likely occluded?
explanation: The left middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral surface of the hemisphere, including the motor areas for the face and arm and Broca's area in the dominant frontal lobe, so occlusion causes contralateral face and arm weakness with expressive aphasia. The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface, where the leg is represented.

stem: A 70-year-old man suddenly develops weakness and numbness of the left leg, with only mild weakness of the left arm and no facial weakness. Which artery is most likely occluded?
explanation: The leg and foot areas of the motor and sensory cortex lie on the medial surface of the hemisphere in the paracentral lobule, which is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery; occlusion causes contralateral leg-predominant weakness and sensory loss. Middle cerebral occlusion affects the face and arm more than the leg.

stem: A 63-year-old woman notices that she bumps into objects on her left side. Examination shows a left homonymous hemianopia with sparing of central (macular) vision, and no limb weakness. Which artery is most likely occluded?
explanation: The right posterior cerebral artery supplies the right occipital (visual) cortex, which receives the left visual field; macular sparing occurs because the occipital pole often receives collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery. A right middle cerebral artery stroke would typically also cause left-sided weakness.

stem: A 58-year-old man has sudden vertigo, hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. He has loss of pain and temperature sensation on the right side of his face and on the left side of his body, a small right pupil with ptosis, and right-sided limb ataxia. Limb power is normal. Which artery is most likely occluded?
options: Left vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Right anterior spinal artery supplying the medial medulla
Right vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar artery
explanation: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome results from occlusion of the vertebral artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery on the side of the lesion. It damages the spinal trigeminal nucleus (ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss), the spinothalamic tract (contralateral body), the nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia and hoarseness), descending sympathetic fibres (Horner's) and cerebellar pathways. The corticospinal tract lies medially and is spared, so there is no weakness.

stem: A 60-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension has sudden weakness of the left face, arm and leg with no sensory loss, visual field defect or speech problem. MRI shows a small infarct in the posterior limb of the right internal capsule. Which vessels supply this area?
options: Cortical branches of the anterior cerebral artery
Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery
Pontine branches of the basilar artery
Calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery
explanation: The posterior limb of the internal capsule, which carries the corticospinal fibres, is supplied mainly by the lenticulostriate arteries from the middle cerebral artery (with the anterior choroidal artery). These small penetrating arteries are damaged by hypertension, causing lacunar infarcts such as pure motor stroke. Cortical branches supply the surface of the hemisphere.

stem: A 40-year-old woman develops a sudden 'worst ever' headache with neck stiffness, and CT shows subarachnoid blood. Angiography shows a berry aneurysm. At which site do berry aneurysms most commonly occur?
explanation: Berry aneurysms arise at branch points of the circle of Willis, most often at the junction of the anterior communicating artery with the anterior cerebral arteries, followed by the posterior communicating artery origin and the middle cerebral bifurcation. Posterior circulation aneurysms are less common.

stem: A 65-year-old man has a ptosis with the right eye turned down and out and a dilated right pupil, together with weakness of the left face, arm and leg. Where is the lesion?
options: Right side of the midbrain (cerebral peduncle)
explanation: Weber's syndrome results from a lesion in the ventral midbrain, damaging the emerging oculomotor nerve fibres (ipsilateral third nerve palsy) and the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres in the cerebral peduncle, which cross below this level (contralateral hemiplegia). A pontine lesion would involve the sixth or seventh nerve rather than the third.

stem: A 20-year-old man is stabbed in the back, hemisecting the right side of his spinal cord at T8. Which pattern of deficit is expected below the level of the injury?
options: Right weakness, right proprioceptive loss, right pain and temperature loss
Left weakness, left proprioceptive loss, right pain and temperature loss
Right weakness, right proprioceptive loss, left pain and temperature loss
Bilateral weakness, intact proprioception, bilateral pain and temperature loss
explanation: In Brown-Séquard syndrome, the corticospinal tract and dorsal columns, which cross in the brainstem, are damaged on the same side, causing ipsilateral weakness and loss of proprioception and vibration. The spinothalamic tract has already crossed within a segment or two of entry, so pain and temperature are lost on the opposite side.

stem: A 32-year-old man has burned his hands while cooking without feeling pain. He has loss of pain and temperature sensation over both shoulders and arms in a cape distribution, with preserved light touch and joint position sense, and wasting of the small hand muscles. Which structure is damaged first by the most likely lesion?
options: Dorsal columns of the cervical cord
Lateral corticospinal tracts in the lateral funiculus
Dorsal root ganglia of the cervical nerves
Crossing fibres in the anterior white commissure
explanation: A syrinx (fluid-filled cavity) in the central cervical cord first damages the spinothalamic fibres crossing in the anterior white commissure, producing a dissociated, cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved dorsal column sensation. Expansion into the anterior horns causes wasting of the hand muscles.

stem: A 55-year-old strict vegetarian woman has tingling feet, an unsteady gait that is worse in the dark, absent ankle jerks and extensor plantar responses. Her Romberg test is positive. Which spinal cord tracts are mainly affected?
options: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
explanation: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord from vitamin B12 deficiency affects the dorsal columns (loss of proprioception and vibration, positive Romberg test) and the lateral corticospinal tracts (extensor plantars), often with a peripheral neuropathy that abolishes the ankle jerks. Spinothalamic sensation is relatively spared.

stem: After repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm, a 70-year-old man cannot move his legs and has lost pain and temperature sensation below the umbilicus, but vibration and joint position sense in his feet are normal. Which artery's territory has been affected?
explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord, including the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts; in the thoracolumbar region it depends heavily on a radicular feeder (artery of Adamkiewicz) that can be lost during aortic surgery. The dorsal columns are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries and are spared.

stem: Which nucleus provides the preganglionic parasympathetic fibres that constrict the pupil in the light reflex?
explanation: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus travel in the oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion, whose postganglionic fibres supply the sphincter pupillae. The pretectal nucleus receives the light signal and relays it to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, explaining the consensual response.

stem: A 50-year-old man has a tumour at the foramen ovale. When he opens his mouth, his jaw deviates to the left, and the left temporalis and masseter are wasted. Which nerve is affected?
explanation: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve leaves the skull through the foramen ovale and supplies the muscles of mastication. The lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle forwards on opening, so if the left is paralysed, the right pushes the jaw towards the left, the side of the lesion. The facial nerve does not supply muscles of mastication.

stem: After middle ear surgery, a 30-year-old woman notices loss of taste over the front of her tongue on one side, but her facial movements are normal. Which nerve was injured?
explanation: The chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and crosses the middle ear on the tympanic membrane, so it may be damaged during ear surgery while facial movement is unaffected. The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the posterior third, and the greater petrosal nerve carries lacrimal secretomotor fibres and palatal taste.

stem: Which cranial nerve carries both taste and general sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue?
options: Lingual branch of the mandibular nerve
explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies both taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, including the vallate papillae. In the anterior two-thirds, general sensation is carried by the lingual nerve and taste by the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve.

stem: A 45-year-old man has diplopia on looking to the right, and his right eye cannot move laterally. Which muscle is paralysed?
explanation: The right lateral rectus, supplied by the right abducens nerve, abducts the right eye; its paralysis prevents the eye moving outwards and causes horizontal diplopia worst on looking to the right. The right medial rectus would affect adduction, on looking to the left.

stem: A medical student is testing the superior oblique muscle in isolation. In which position of the eye is its depressing action best tested?
explanation: Superior oblique pulls from the trochlea at the front of the orbit; when the eye is adducted, its line of pull aligns with the visual axis, so it acts purely as a depressor. In abduction, inferior rectus is the main depressor, so superior oblique is tested by asking the patient to look down and in.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, loss of the gag reflex on the left and weakness of the left trapezius and sternocleidomastoid. Tongue movements are normal. Through which opening do all the affected nerves pass?
explanation: The glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves leave the skull together through the jugular foramen, so a lesion there (for example a glomus tumour) causes this combination (jugular foramen syndrome). The hypoglossal nerve leaves through the hypoglossal canal, which explains the normal tongue.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has brief stabbing pains over her cheek and upper lip triggered by brushing her teeth. Through which foramen does the affected division of the trigeminal nerve leave the skull?
explanation: Pain over the cheek and upper lip lies in the maxillary division (V2), which leaves the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum. The ophthalmic division passes through the superior orbital fissure, the mandibular division through the foramen ovale, and the middle meningeal artery through the foramen spinosum.

stem: A newborn delivered with forceps has weakness of the whole right side of the face, with difficulty closing the right eye. Why is the facial nerve especially vulnerable in the newborn?
options: The mastoid process is absent, so the nerve lies superficially
The facial canal in the temporal bone is not yet ossified
The parotid gland does not yet cover the nerve's branches
The nerve fibres are not yet myelinated at birth
explanation: At birth the mastoid process is absent, so the facial nerve emerges from the stylomastoid foramen close to the surface of the side of the head, where forceps can compress it. The mastoid process develops during the first two years and then protects the nerve.

stem: During thyroidectomy, the surgeon ligates the superior thyroid artery. From which artery does it usually arise?
explanation: The superior thyroid artery is usually the first branch of the external carotid artery and descends to the upper pole with the external laryngeal nerve. The inferior thyroid artery comes from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.

stem: After a total thyroidectomy, a 38-year-old woman has persistent hypocalcaemia. The surgeon explains that the inferior parathyroid glands are more variable in position than the superior ones and may even lie in the superior mediastinum. What is the embryological reason?
options: They arise from the fourth pouch and do not descend
They arise from the second pouch with the palatine tonsil
They arise from the ultimobranchial body with the C cells
They arise from the third pouch and descend with the thymus
explanation: The inferior parathyroids develop from the dorsal part of the third pharyngeal pouch alongside the thymus (ventral part) and are pulled down with it, so they may stop anywhere along this path or end up in the mediastinum. The superior parathyroids come from the fourth pouch, migrate less and are more constant in position.

stem: Which muscles bound the carotid triangle of the neck?
options: Anterior border of trapezius, sternocleidomastoid and clavicle
Sternocleidomastoid, superior belly of omohyoid and posterior belly of digastric
Both bellies of digastric and the lower border of the mandible
Sternocleidomastoid, midline of the neck and superior belly of omohyoid
explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded by the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, the superior belly of omohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric; it contains the carotid bifurcation, where the pulse and carotid sinus are found. The triangle bounded by sternocleidomastoid, the midline and omohyoid is the muscular triangle.

stem: An anaesthetist performs a superficial cervical plexus block for a neck procedure. Near which surface landmark do the cutaneous branches of the plexus emerge?
options: Midpoint of the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid
Upper border of the thyroid cartilage in the midline
explanation: The lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves all wind around the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid at about its midpoint (sometimes called the nerve point of the neck), so local anaesthetic infiltrated there blocks the superficial cervical plexus. The spinal accessory nerve also emerges near this point.

stem: A 50-year-old man has bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsies after thyroid surgery and develops stridor. Paralysis of which muscle, the only one that opens the vocal cords, explains the airway obstruction?
explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal cords; with both recurrent laryngeal nerves damaged, the cords lie close to the midline and cannot open, causing stridor and possibly needing a tracheostomy. The lateral cricoarytenoid and arytenoid muscles are adductors, and cricothyroid tenses the cords.

stem: A baby is born in a rural hospital with a unilateral cleft of the upper lip lateral to the philtrum. Failure of fusion of which embryological structures causes this defect?
options: Palatal shelves of the maxillary prominences
Maxillary prominence and medial nasal prominence
explanation: The upper lip forms when each maxillary prominence fuses with the merged medial nasal prominences (which form the philtrum); failure on one side gives a unilateral cleft lip lateral to the philtrum. Failure of the palatal shelves to fuse causes cleft palate.

stem: A 12-year-old boy in Hyderabad has recurrent nosebleeds in summer. Most such bleeds arise from a vascular plexus in which part of the nose?
options: Posterior part of the lateral wall
Anterior inferior part of the nasal septum
explanation: Kiesselbach's plexus in Little's area on the anterior inferior nasal septum is formed by branches of the sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine and superior labial arteries; it is exposed to dry air and trauma and is the source of most anterior epistaxis. Posterior bleeds, usually from the sphenopalatine artery, are less common and more serious.

stem: A 59-year-old right-handed man after a stroke understands speech but speaks slowly and with great effort, in short phrases. Which area is damaged?
options: Inferior frontal gyrus of the left hemisphere
Superior temporal gyrus of the left hemisphere
Angular gyrus of the right hemisphere
Precentral gyrus of the right hemisphere
explanation: Broca's area, in the posterior inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere, is needed for speech production; damage causes non-fluent expressive aphasia with preserved comprehension. Damage to the left superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's area) causes fluent speech with poor comprehension.

stem: A 70-year-old woman after a stroke speaks fluently but her speech makes no sense, and she cannot follow simple commands. Which area is most likely damaged?
explanation: Wernicke's area in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere is needed to understand language; damage causes fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension (receptive aphasia). Lesions of the inferior frontal gyrus cause non-fluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension.

stem: A 45-year-old man has a tumour in the left cerebellar hemisphere. Which sign would you expect?
explanation: Each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates the limbs on the same side because its outflow crosses to the opposite thalamus and cortex, whose corticospinal fibres cross back. A left cerebellar lesion therefore causes left-sided ataxia, intention tremor and past-pointing. Resting tremor is a feature of Parkinson's disease.

stem: A 65-year-old man has a resting tremor, rigidity and slowness of movement. Loss of dopaminergic neurones in which structure underlies his condition?
explanation: Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta, which project to the striatum (nigrostriatal pathway). Caudate degeneration is characteristic of Huntington's disease, and subthalamic lesions cause hemiballismus.

stem: A 72-year-old diabetic woman develops sudden violent, flinging movements of her right arm and leg. A small infarct is found. Where is it most likely to be?
explanation: Hemiballismus results from a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, often a small lacunar infarct, which removes its excitatory drive on the internal globus pallidus and releases the thalamus and motor cortex. Basal ganglia effects are expressed through the ipsilateral cortex, so the movements are on the opposite side of the body.

stem: A 6-month-old baby has an enlarging head. CT shows dilated lateral and third ventricles but a normal-sized fourth ventricle. Where is the obstruction?
explanation: The cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain connects the third and fourth ventricles; aqueductal stenosis dilates the ventricles above it while the fourth ventricle stays normal. Obstruction at the fourth ventricle outlets would also dilate the fourth ventricle, and failure of absorption at the arachnoid granulations dilates all ventricles (communicating hydrocephalus).

stem: A 42-year-old man with a large central disc prolapse at L4/L5 develops urinary retention, numbness around the anus and perineum, and bilateral leg weakness. Which structure is compressed?
explanation: In adults the spinal cord ends at about L1–L2, so below that level the canal contains the cauda equina, the lumbar and sacral nerve roots; a central disc prolapse compresses the sacral roots, causing saddle anaesthesia and bladder dysfunction. This is a surgical emergency. The spinal cord itself is not present at L4/L5.

stem: A 50-year-old man has lost vibration and joint position sense in his legs and sways when he closes his eyes while standing. His arms are normal. Which tract is most affected?
explanation: The fasciculus gracilis, the medial part of the dorsal columns, carries proprioception, vibration and fine touch from the lower limbs and lower trunk; its damage causes sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg test. The fasciculus cuneatus carries the same modalities from the upper limbs, which are normal here.

stem: A 30-year-old man has a tumour compressing the left lateral funiculus of the spinal cord at the T6 segment. Where would you expect loss of pain and temperature sensation?
options: On the right, from about two segments below the lesion downwards
On the left, from the level of the lesion downwards
On both sides at T6 only
On the right, from the level of the shoulder downwards
explanation: Pain and temperature fibres ascend one or two segments before crossing in the anterior white commissure to the contralateral lateral spinothalamic tract. A left-sided tract lesion at T6 therefore causes loss on the right side, starting about one or two segments below the lesion. A bilateral band at one level suggests a central lesion such as a syrinx.

stem: Where do most fibres of the corticospinal tract cross to the opposite side?
options: In the anterior white commissure of the cord
In the pyramidal decussation of the lower medulla
explanation: About 85–90 % of corticospinal fibres cross in the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract, which is why a lesion above the medulla causes contralateral weakness and a cord lesion causes ipsilateral weakness. The anterior white commissure carries crossing spinothalamic fibres.

stem: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced in the ventricles and must return to the venous circulation. Where is most CSF absorbed?
options: Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricles
Arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus
Ependymal lining of the third ventricle
Straight sinus through the great cerebral vein
explanation: CSF is produced mainly by the choroid plexuses and absorbed through arachnoid villi and granulations that project into the dural venous sinuses, especially the superior sagittal sinus. Blocked absorption here, as after meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage, causes communicating hydrocephalus.

stem: In the circle of Willis, which vessel connects the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery?
explanation: The posterior communicating artery links each internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery, joining the anterior and posterior circulations. The anterior communicating artery joins the two anterior cerebral arteries.

stem: A 25-year-old man with a large right extradural haematoma becomes less responsive, and his right pupil becomes fixed and dilated. Which part of the brain is compressing the right oculomotor nerve?
explanation: A supratentorial mass pushes the medial temporal lobe (uncus) through the tentorial notch, where it compresses the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve; its superficial pupillary fibres are affected first, giving a fixed dilated pupil. Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses the medulla and causes respiratory arrest.

stem: A 60-year-old woman has weakness of her right arm and leg and loss of vibration and joint position sense on the right side of her body. Her tongue deviates to the left when protruded and the left side of the tongue is wasted. Where is the lesion?
explanation: Medial medullary syndrome, usually from anterior spinal or vertebral artery branch occlusion, damages the pyramid (contralateral hemiparesis), the medial lemniscus (contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration) and the hypoglossal nerve or nucleus (ipsilateral tongue weakness, deviating towards the lesion). Lateral medullary lesions spare power and the tongue.
